title: Hawaii Happiness Symposium Part 2 with Jane Choe
summary: The Hawaii happiness inquiry continues with David Choe's mother, Jane Choe, and Critter Fleming. Jane begins with `I Am Happy` in four languages, connects family history under Japanese colonial rule to welcome rather than inherited blame, and describes late-life art made on anything available. That art becomes a test of creation without credentials: Jane works quickly and abundantly, Critter prepares seven paintings carefully, and David refuses to make either method subordinate to professional training. Airport pickup, kimchi, rice, diabetes, family travel and snorkeling lead to the episode's title-like comic line, `the turtle said yes with her eyes`; the archive keeps the joke and makes the conservation boundary explicit—wildlife cannot consent and NOAA says not to touch sea turtles. The central interview contrasts Jane's Christian happiness practice with David's attraction to chaos. Faith, apology, silence, prayer, forgiveness and `you are the masterpiece` coexist with his abandonment at age three, the LA riots, self-destructive behavior, therapy and a childhood full of hair pulling, police threats, scared-straight performances, physical fights and contradictory lessons about stealing. Mother and son openly disagree about the cornfield memory, making memory divergence part of the record rather than a problem to smooth over. The ending turns criticism and adversity into free teachers, then closes in prayer and improvised song. Every idea—including slurs, spiritual claims, body mockery, wildlife contact, self-harm language and child punishment—remains. Clinical, historical and conservation annotations sit beside the transcript instead of replacing it, private relatives and discovery trails remain protected, and no transcript turn receives a speaker name.
source_notes: The only cleaner edit is real decoder failure: a 6.26-second opening segment repeats `school` about 218 times with compression 38.0976. The clean artifact retains an indistinct-audio marker rather than pretending the region was silence.
All eight automated vocabulary edits are safe local names/titles: David Choe, Jane Choe, DVDASA and Anthony Bourdain: Parts Unknown. The review queue is empty.

NOAA says Hawaiian sea turtles are protected, should never be touched, and should generally be viewed from at least ten feet. Some NPS-managed sites request twenty feet. Eye contact is not permission: https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/s3/2025-06/marine-viewing-guidelines-rackcard-jpn-eng-2023-final-web.pdf and https://www.nps.gov/kaho/learn/nature/turtles.htm

CDC says diabetes can reduce blood flow and damage nerves, making wounds more infection-prone and harder to heal. The episode's broad statement is directionally grounded but should not be generalized to every injury: https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/diabetes-complications/diabetes-and-your-feet.html

The American Diabetes Association includes brown rice among minimally processed carbohydrate foods that can fit diabetes meal planning. Brown/black rice is not categorically forbidden; portion and individual treatment matter: https://diabetes.org/food-nutrition/understanding-carbs

APA defines EMDR as eye movement desensitization and reprocessing, a structured psychotherapy used for traumatic memories/PTSD—not `rapid eye movement therapy`: https://www.apa.org/topics/psychotherapy/emdr-therapy-ptsd
Statements about God, Satan, angels, prayer, scripture, happiness and adversity remain Jane's theology. The editorial record neither deletes them nor converts them into clinical claims.

Claims about early childhood, abandonment, abuse, crime, family motive and the cornfield/police events are remembered accounts. The episode itself preserves conflicting memories and should not be flattened into one adjudicated version.
Zero diarized turns and zero identity windows mean that explicit participant presence cannot support named transcript dialogue.

connections.why: The same Hawaii stay moves from Harry and Critter's temperament to Jane's Christian practice.
A happiness song carries Japanese, Chinese, English and Korean family memory.
Forced Japanese names coexist with hospitality toward later Japanese-American children.
Retirement, museums and a family exhibition make art a lived activity rather than credential.
Jane's volume and Critter's preparation are treated as different valid methods.
The show is proof that fear and lack of training need not precede every artwork.
Handmade art matters more than purchasable objects to someone with material abundance.
Raw passion is linked to the chef's stated preference for uncredentialed initiative.
Difficulty painting noses becomes an identifiable formal choice rather than paralysis.
The island joins rehab memory, quiet, family travel and wildlife encounter.
Family food planning mixes valid concern with an overly broad rice prohibition.
A smaller hike substitutes for a strenuous bucket-list journey amid falls and diabetes.
The joke about eyes saying yes repeats the archive's larger problem of inferring permission.
Elevator laughter offers a contained alternative to suppressing joy or forcing an audience.
Solomon's wives become a religious warning that more does not yield peace.
Jane dates her move from complaint toward peace to becoming Christian in 1977.
Jane says reported hurt can warrant apology even when she did not understand causing it.
Being sent away at three organizes later fear of preciousness, safety and loss.
Family separation and public destruction become a shared theory that everything can vanish.
The blank-computer metaphor captures felt importance but overstates developmental certainty.
Jane's theology turns verbal restraint into spiritual boundary-setting.
The religious warning not to voice darkness must not suppress crisis or clinical help-seeking.
Hair-pulling called `the punk` ironically precedes the sons' attraction to punk music.
A therapist's formulation joins childhood instability to adult comfort with destruction.
A named structured trauma therapy appears beside prayer rather than being replaced by it.
`You are the masterpiece` answers the fear that external work and status can be destroyed.
Day/night, permission/theft and lesson/adventure remain different family versions.
Enemies and failure are reframed as free teachers without making harm necessary or welcome.
